title: Who gets thrown out of the cache?
hook: The cache is full and a new item arrives. Does the oldest arrival go, or someone else?

knows: that fetching from far away is slow
keeping a few things close at hand
doesNotKnow: what a cache is and that it has a fixed number of slots
that caches usually evict by recent use, not by arrival

misconception: A full cache drops whatever arrived first.
objective: The learner can trace a least-recently-used cache: on A, B, C, A, D with 3 slots, the repeat request for A refreshes it, so D evicts B, while a first-in rule would evict A.

claims.text: With 3 slots and requests A, B, C, A, D, the least-recently-used rule evicts B when D arrives.
claims.source: Demo.tsx simulate(5, 'lru'): last uses B = 2, C = 3, A = 4; B has the oldest last use. Builder also ran an independent LRU in Node: evicted [B], 4 misses.

claims.text: On the same stream a first-in, first-out rule evicts A, the oldest arrival, even though A was just requested.
claims.source: Demo.tsx simulate(5, 'fifo'): arrivals A = 1, B = 2, C = 3; A evicted. Builder ran an independent FIFO in Node: evicted [A].

claims.text: Asking for an item that is already in the cache is a hit and makes it the most recently used.
claims.source: Definition of LRU replacement: Silberschatz, Galvin and Gagne, Operating System Concepts, 10th ed., 10.4.4 'LRU Page Replacement'.

claims.text: Things used recently tend to be used again soon, so operating systems and web caches use the least-recently-used rule or cheap approximations of it.
claims.source: Principle of temporal locality: Denning, 'The locality principle', CACM 48(7), 2005; Silberschatz et al. 10.4.4 (LRU approximates the optimal policy by using the recent past to predict the near future). 'Usually' is a tendency for workloads with locality, not a guarantee.

claims.text: Operating systems and web caches use the least-recently-used rule or cheap approximations of it.
claims.source: Silberschatz et al. 10.4.5 'LRU-Approximation Page Replacement' (reference bits, second-chance/clock); Redis documentation 'Key eviction' (allkeys-lru, an approximated LRU).

claims.text: On the stream A, B, C, A, D with 3 slots, both rules score 1 hit and 4 misses; afterwards a request for B hits under first in, first out (it kept B) and misses under least recently used, while a request for A hits under least recently used and misses under first in, first out.
claims.source: Simulated in the stage: LRU leaves {A, C, D}; FIFO leaves {B, C, D}. The only hit is A at step 4 under both.

recall.question: A cache holds 2 items and uses least recently used. Requests: X, Y, X, Z. Which item is evicted when Z arrives?
options: Y, because it was used longest ago
recall.why: The second request for X refreshed it, so Y has gone longest without use and is the one evicted.
